rep.name: Andrew Musial

The 06/24 team meeting establishes that Andrew Jin is a former coach whose Fathom account the current closer is recording into — 'there's a call from Andrew Jin, the former coach' / 'it's weird that he's still somehow able to get in to a Fathom that isn't his.' The rep on this call is Andrew Musial, per the Drive folder and batch record.

setter.name: Kim Forbes-Sobers
setter.evidence: Okay, Jean-Philippe, I spoke with Kim. You spoke with him, I think, yesterday or a couple of days ago. — identified from the transcript; this title carries no setter suffix. The prospect separately reports that Kim no-showed an earlier scheduled call with him.

prospect.name: Jean-Philippe Rifaat
prospect.occupation: Works in fashion — product development and sourcing for a brand. 'I work in the source, so I develop the, you know, the product. And I know exactly what it costs to make it, to develop it.' In the office almost every day.
prospect.family_status: Not disclosed. He described his approach to training as solitary — 'I'm on this on my own. I'm here alone today, and I will be for the rest of my life, you know? It's just me' — but that was about doing it for himself, and no household composition was stated.
prospect.training_background: Long-standing gym-goer on a EUR 95/month 'train more, pay less' membership in Amsterdam, contracted until February and not cancellable. Previously had a personal trainer with a weekly session, paying EUR 250/month including the membership. Owns kettlebells that have sat in his garden since COVID; trained with them sporadically but never consistently. Has followed Trevor on social media for several years. Plant-based for eight-plus years and running 18:6 intermittent fasting for several months. Self-describes as fit and very active for his age.

signals: Caveat on the fit: the 'cheap alternative that genuinely worked' clause does not hold — his EUR 95 gym and his own kettlebells demonstrably have not worked for him. On profile he reads as the_optimizer (fit, successful, good-to-great, comfortable with premium spend); on behaviour he is a bargain hunter, and the behaviour is what decided the call.
Self-directed to the point of identity: 'I'm a very independent person. I've always been like a lonely rider in a way' and 'I don't really follow the crowd. Never have in my life.'
Prices the offer professionally rather than emotionally — he develops product for a fashion brand and reasons from cost to make: 'I know exactly what it costs to make it, to develop it.'
Confirmed capacity and still refused on value: 'I can pay the 6K. That we know' and 'I think it's a bit overpriced, well, not a bit, I think it's very overpriced.'
Converted the price to a monthly rate within seconds of hearing it — '1,000 a month' — and benchmarked it against a EUR 250/month personal trainer.

goals.text: Have a programme to follow so he does not have to think about what to do when he trains
Set himself a standard and actually hold to it — a purely personal achievement, nothing to do with anyone else
Feel better physically and, through that, mentally — 'those go very much hand in hand'
Maintain the body and function he has as he ages — 'the older you get, the more actually you have to do'
Train in a more dynamic way than the gym allows, ideally barefoot in his own garden rather than in a commercial gym

pains.text: Kettlebells have sat in his garden since COVID; he has trained with them some but never consistently because there is no plan to follow
Frustration and disappointment with himself over discipline — 'it's all about discipline, and I haven't had the discipline, and I'm still looking for...'
The gym is repetitive and the environment alienating — 'I can walk you naked, no one will notice... It's dead. It's like a mortuary. Only the bodies are moving.'
Strong aversion to phone-mediated training; filming himself training and sending it is 'the least organic thing'
Automated and AI-written follow-up messaging actively repelled him from the brand

objections.raw_quote: Videoing myself, training, sending, okay, if I commit something, I will do it, but it's definitely not something I like to do, because I don't like phones.
objections.rep_response: Narrowed it to the learning phase only — 'especially in the beginning phase, when you're going to be learning the movements... two, three months in, probably you will not need it' — offered filming on a laptop in his garden instead, then asked directly whether it was a deal breaker.

objections.raw_quote: It's very American, it's super American, how this is, I keep getting these messages, it actually turns me totally off, I already, again, I get these messages, and it's like, da-da-da, and I said, is this, again, another automated?
objections.rep_response: Confirmed it is AI, then justified the automation on operational grounds — 'You wouldn't believe how many people forget, miss the messages... And it's a waste of my precious time too.' Did not address the brand mismatch itself.

objections.raw_quote: I'm not cheap at I like to invest in what I believe in, and I do believe in this program, but I think it's a bit overpriced, well, not a bit, I think it's very overpriced.
objections.rep_response: Asked 'comparing to what?', separated the model from a personal trainer, said he would lower the price if he could but it was not in his power, then reframed to delayed gratification and a deathbed frame, and finally improvised a one-month trial at $1,200 or $1,500.

objections.raw_quote: out of the three blocks that you mentioned, the three, the third one is the one that I'm looking for.
objections.rep_response: Refused to unbundle — 'it is designed like this because it cannot be separate' and 'if you would be only doing workouts, like he wouldn't have such amazing results because the nutrition is a crucial part of the transformation.'
Did not run the think-about-it play. Sent the financing link instead — 'let me send you this link. Check it out and let me know if this is something in your ballpark or not.'

objections.raw_quote: Maybe in a year's time, I'm willing to spend 6K in this, or something like this. But at this point, no. It's too much.
objections.rep_response: Ran the closest thing to a scripted play on the call — 'But what's going to be the difference in your time from now?', 'And in a year's time, it's not going to be too much?', 'Come on, let's be serious. What will change in your mindset in one year?' — then abandoned it when the prospect deflected with a joke.

tiers.note: Improvised 'love it or leave it' trial month, credited toward the six-month tier
Improvised trial month priced against the three-month tier

offer.payment_plan_terms: Rep sent a third-party financing link in the Zoom chat that can split the fee over up to 12 months, and named Klarna as the comparable product while stating Primal uses a different provider. The prospect opened it and read it correctly: 'So this is just splitting it into... But at the end, it's, of course, same, you still pay $6,000 for six months.' No plan was agreed. Separately the rep offered a 4K three-month start with a 2K top-up to reach six months.
offer.guarantee_mentioned: Trevor guarantees, like, when you start the six months journey with him, and for example, you start with an 8K kettlebell, you will in six months add at least 8K to your baseline. That's a guarantee. And if you don't do that in six months and you follow through and everything, he will work with you for free until you do. And that's a paper on agreement that you sign.

prospect_financials.note: No figures were asked for or disclosed — none of the six scripted financial-picture questions ran. Capacity was confirmed verbally only: 'I can pay the 6K. That we know.' He also carries a EUR 95/month gym contract until February, roughly EUR 600 across the six months, which he raised as a parallel cost.

evidence: Final position, unchanged after every rebuttal: 'there's a price for everything, and I personally don't think that it's worth for me to spend $6,000 on maintaining my body for $6,000.'
Rep accepted it: 'Okay, fair enough. I've shown you everything, what we can, how we can help you, but as I said, it's up to you, it's not my decision.'
Refused the improvised one-month trial too: 'Yeah, but something tells me no.' 'My gut feeling. About what? About the price.'

Counter-evidence: he believed in the product throughout — 'there's no doubt in the program, no doubt in Trevor and his method and his quality. And I don't have a doubt in you or what you've, how you've presented' — and he confirmed he could afford it. This is a pure value rejection, not an affordability one.
Counter-evidence: he left the door open — 'Maybe in a year's time, I'm willing to spend 6K in this' and 'who knows? Our paths will cross. Never say never.'
outcome.next_step: None. No follow-up was booked and no re-engagement date was set.

notable.note: Four prices below the stated offer appeared on this call: $4,000 for three months, a $2,000 top-up, and a one-month 'love it or leave it' trial at $1,200 or $1,500. The rep had said eleven minutes earlier 'Look, if I could do it, I would lower the price for you. But I cannot. It's not in my power', then produced a new tier anyway. The $1,200 figure matches the internal minimum-before-onboarding number stated in the 06/22 team meeting. Two other findings a principal should see: the prospect reports that the setter no-showed an earlier scheduled call and left him waiting fifteen minutes, and the automated follow-up messaging was identified by him as AI and named as a reason he distrusts the brand. Finally, no health, injury or movement-limitation question was asked at any point of a 55-year-old being sold ballistic kettlebell training — the baseline phase was almost entirely skipped.
